primary_topics: Appendix A of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's tribute 'A Salute to My Mentor,' delivered June 17, 2001 at the launch of former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's book 'A Journey of Struggle and Hope,' recounting how Salonga became his lifelong 'guru' and role model

The formative biographical narrative: the 1956 Far Eastern University law-student strike, where the new 36-year-old dean Salonga (a Yale-and-Harvard graduate and bar topnotcher) singlehandedly faced and turned back a thousand protesting students -- the moment CJP found his model 'not only in my chosen career but... in my life as a whole'

CJP's own student and bar-exam story under Salonga's mentorship (Latin honors, 'most outstanding student,' the storm-and-illness 1960 bar he nearly quit but passed sixth-highest), and the three trying years (1992-1995) of seven failed Judicial and Bar Council screenings, through which Salonga sustained him with Romans 8:28 until his appointment by President Ramos

Salonga's enduring teaching that CJP says he tries to echo -- 'that law cannot be separated from life' -- and the treasured life lesson distinguishing the things money CAN buy (food, shelter, recreation, a car and a house) from the far more important things money CANNOT buy (excellence, integrity, honor, dignity, and a reverential love for God)
sub_topics: The occasion: remarks at the Valle Verde Country Club on June 17, 2001, launching Salonga's autobiography 'A Journey of Struggle and Hope,' elucidating an incident mentioned on its page 75

The 1956 FEU strike: a freshman among a thousand striking law students protesting the 'precipitate and unjustified retirement' of the beloved old dean; the new dean Salonga, 36, a Yale and Harvard graduate and bar topnotcher, faced the hostile crowd and 'in thirty minutes flat' sent them back to class, convinced of his 'wisdom, honesty, sincerity and good faith'

CJP as student leader: president of both the FEU student council and the National Union of Students of the Philippines; Salonga, his professor in evidence and corporation law, kept reminding him that academics came first, calling on him to recite at the height of his activities -- so he graduated with Latin honors and as 'most outstanding student'

The 1960 bar examinations: sick and confined at the FEU Hospital, CJP waded knee-deep on R. Papa Street to the exam venue; after a 'lackluster' first day he wanted to quit, but Salonga 'would not hear of it,' and he passed sixth-highest

Joining Salonga's law firm (with partners Sedfrey A. Ordoñez, Pedro L. Yap and Neptali A. Gonzales), where he learned 'the rudiments of law practice' and 'the life-defining values of integrity, prudence and fairness'

Salonga the man: a model who 'taught by example, not by words'; a dedicated husband, caring father, faithful friend and 'devoted man of God' who never compromised principle 'in exchange for friendship, kinship, relationship, wealth or power' and lived 'an almost ascetic life' (no smoking, drinking or gambling)

Their friendship across faiths: Salonga a devout Protestant and leader of the Cosmopolitan Church, CJP 'a fledgling Catholic' -- more than four decades of friendship undimmed because 'we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us'

Salonga's honors to CJP: appointing him personal legal counsel during his Senate presidency and concurrently chief legal counsel of the Liberal Party -- 'nothing is more fulfilling... than the honor of being counsel to one's mentor'

The seven JBC rejections: from 1992 to 1995, for each of seven Court vacancies, CJP's name was submitted to and rejected by the Judicial and Bar Council for 'alleged insufficiency of professional competence' and 'alleged transgressions and sins'; Salonga sustained him throughout, reminding him of Romans 8:28, until his eventual nomination and appointment by President Ramos

The two governing teachings: that 'law cannot be separated from life' and should build 'the social edifice'; and the distinction between the things money CAN buy and the far more important things it cannot -- excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and 'a reverential regard and love for God as the Source of all that is true, good and beautiful'

stances.claim: Salonga's most significant teaching 'is not really about the law, as it is about life': while one may rightly desire the necessities money can buy, it is 'far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God' -- the life-credo CJP says he treasures above all.
stances.rhetorical_move: things-money-cannot-buy distinction: distilling a mentor's example into a single transmissible value hierarchy that subordinates material goods to character and faith
stances.confidence: stated as CJP's most treasured personal teaching

stances.claim: Faith differences need not divide deep friendship: Salonga a devout Protestant and CJP a Catholic sustained more than four decades of friendship because 'we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us' -- a model of ecumenical respect grounded in shared values rather than doctrinal agreement.
stances.rhetorical_move: common-ground principle: framing a cross-denominational bond as proof that shared character matters more than sectarian difference
stances.confidence: offered as a lived personal conviction

notable_anecdotes: Facing the mob in thirty minutes: as a freshman caught up in the 1956 FEU strike, CJP watched the new 36-year-old dean Salonga walk alone to the microphone and, with 'a forceful tremolo,' turn a thousand hostile students back to their classrooms in half an hour -- the moment he found his lifelong 'guru.'

Wading to the bar exams: sick and hospitalized days before the 1960 bar, CJP waded knee-deep through floodwaters on R. Papa Street to reach the exam venue and, after a discouraging first day, wanted to quit -- but Salonga 'would not hear of it,' and he placed sixth.

Seven rejections in three years: CJP discloses that from 1992 to 1995 his name was submitted to the Judicial and Bar Council for all seven Court vacancies and rejected each time for 'alleged insufficiency of... competence' and 'alleged transgressions and sins,' with Salonga 'beside me, behind me, and even above me' -- reminding him of Romans 8:28 -- until his eventual appointment by Ramos.

Counsel to one's mentor: CJP calls it 'the greatest honor in my career as a practising lawyer' that Salonga asked him to be his personal legal counsel as Senate President and chief legal counsel of the Liberal Party.

The things money cannot buy: CJP closes by summarizing Salonga's treasured teaching -- that beyond the necessities money can buy, one must aspire for excellence, integrity, honor, dignity, and 'love for God as the Source of all that is true, good and beautiful.'

one_paragraph_summary: Appendix A of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's tribute 'A Salute to My Mentor,' delivered June 17, 2001 at the launch of former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's autobiography 'A Journey of Struggle and Hope.' CJP recounts the moment in 1956 when, a freshman amid a thousand striking Far Eastern University law students, he watched the new 36-year-old dean Salonga -- a Yale and Harvard graduate and bar topnotcher -- walk alone to the microphone and, 'in thirty minutes flat,' turn the hostile crowd back to their classrooms, the moment he found 'the guru who would become my role model not only in my chosen career but... in my life as a whole.' He traces Salonga's mentorship through his own student leadership (president of the FEU council and the National Union of Students), the insistence on academics that won him Latin honors, and the 1960 bar he nearly quit -- sick and wading floodwaters -- but passed sixth-highest at Salonga's urging. He joined Salonga's firm (with partners Ordoñez, Yap and Gonzales), absorbing 'integrity, prudence and fairness,' and describes Salonga as a man who 'taught by example,' lived 'an almost ascetic life,' and never traded principle for 'friendship, kinship, relationship, wealth or power'; their cross-faith friendship (Protestant mentor, Catholic protege) endured four decades because 'we never discuss what separates us, but only what truly binds us.' Most movingly, CJP discloses the seven Judicial and Bar Council rejections he suffered from 1992 to 1995 -- for 'alleged insufficiency of... competence' and 'alleged transgressions and sins' -- through which Salonga sustained him with Romans 8:28 until his appointment by President Ramos. He closes with Salonga's treasured teaching that 'law cannot be separated from life' and that, beyond the things money can buy, it is far more important to aspire for 'the things that money cannot buy, like excellence, integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God.'
